Madam Vice President of the Human Rights Council, distinguished Member State representatives and observers, ladies and gentlemen, Five years ago, when we completed the third cycle of the Universal Periodic Review, we came before this Council to express our firm conviction that the UPR is, in addition to a peer assessment exercise, an opportunity to reflect and for states to evaluate themselves. We then made a commitment to follow up on the recommendations we received. And through our national mechanism, Cimorey Plus, strive to ensure that those recommendations had a real impact on people's lives through our action. Five years on, we come before the council once again, and this body provides us with a particularly valuable opportunity for us to look back on the path we have followed over the past five years. I'd like to recall the circumstances at the outset, recognise the challenges that we've managed to overcome and assess the progress achieved and responsibly take on the recommendations which will guide our work over the next five years. The cycle which is concluding today started off in extraordinary circumstances. In 2021, Paraguay, like every other country, still faced the huge impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Our institutions strove to reorganize their priorities, adopt new forms of work, and focus significant efforts in responding to an unprecedented health, social and economic emergency. The very review which was held here had to be conducted virtually because of the circumstances we faced. As we gradually returned to institutional normality, we faced another challenge, which was to resume and reorganise institutional work in order to implement the recommendations received. And Simore+ played a vital role in this. What started off as a tool for organizing international recommendations has been gradually enhanced to become a true working method for Paraguayan institutions. We have a network of focal points which has enabled us to assign the recommendations, analyze them and link them up to existing public policies and follow up on them throughout the cycle. So this meant that the recommendations were not just commitments made in the UPR, but they found a specific interlocutor among our country's institutions, which would be responsible for turning them into action. This ownership by our institutions of the recommendations was reflected in the way in which we prepared the fourth national report. This was coordinated through Cimore Plus, and some 66 state institutions took part in it. What is particularly relevant is that in this new cycle, Paraguay has once again received recommendations directed at further strengthening the mechanism, its sustainability, and state institutions ability to follow up on recommendations and to participate. During the past five years, we held elections, which led to a new period of government, the renewal of our authorities, the reorganization of our state entities, and the definition of our priorities, programs, and public policies. This obviously poses new challenges for continuing with any state agenda, but it also creates opportunities. The new public policies allowed us to incorporate human rights commitments into the initiatives which started to take shape, and others could be strengthened or redirected. The recommendations continue to offer us a common framework of reference for all our institutions. This means to say that even though they may have different areas of work, they share responsibilities for implementing recommendations. In this regard, one of the strengths of the Universal Periodic Review is exactly its ability to provide continuity. Governments change, structures develop, new needs and responses emerge. Nevertheless, the state remains responsible. There is also a roadmap which allows us to follow up on the commitments which go beyond the term of one government. Madam Vice-President, as we look back over this cycle, we can see some significant progress in various walks. One of the areas was exactly the strengthening of our human rights institutions. Last year, the Ombudsman's Office recovered its A rating, as it was once again recognized as being in line with the Paris Principles. This was one of the areas of progress that Paraguay highlighted during our review in May and was recognized in turn by a number of different delegations. During this period, my country also extended its international human rights commitments. This included our ratification of the UNESCO Convention on Combating Discrimination in Education, and we also acceded to the Inter-American Convention on Protecting the Human Rights of Older Persons. Now, when it comes to economic and social rights, we launched a national school food program, which currently provides a daily meal to over 1 million pupils and has been implemented in all 263 districts in my country. Now, this is a policy which doesn't only contribute to the right to food, but also fosters children staying longer at school, good nutrition and well-being. We've also overhauled the Paraguayan prison system, We've reorganised the places of detention and we have separated convicts from those who are in pre-trial detention. We've built new premises, trained our prison staff and we have a management model which strives to bring together security, dignity and social rehabilitation. These are major changes which are ongoing, and we realise that we still face significant challenges in this area. Now, I could detail a lot more progress which has been achieved over the past five years, but our aim is not just to present our achievements as exclusively being the result of the UPR. All the progress that we make is the result of national decisions, developing public policies and constant work of a number of institutions and public officials. What we do want to recognize is the value of the peer review mechanism of the UPR. The UPR compels us to analyze our work at home, to organize what we have achieved, to measure progress, to transparently recognize what we haven't yet achieved and see how other states look on the situation in our country. So this is a way of being able to look at each other respectfully, constructively, and so all states without exception are assessed through the same exercise and thus we contribute to mutually improve our systems for promoting and protecting human rights. This is one of the greatest values of the mechanism for Paraguay. On the 6th of May of this year, Paraguay came before the working group for its fourth review. 85 delegations took part in the interactive dialogue. We listened to recognition of the progress we've achieved, observations about ongoing challenges, a number of proposals about actions which we could take as part of our efforts over the next few years. Thus, I would like to express our sincere thanks to each and every one of the states that devoted time to studying the situation in Paraguay and taking part in the review. We'd like to thank those who recognize our progress, those who encouraged us to go further, and those who highlighted outstanding challenges and made recommendations with a view to contributing to our country's efforts. I would also like to thank Ecuador, Kuwait and Slovenia, the members of our troika, for their work. I would also like to thank the Council presidency, the secretariat and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights for their support throughout the process. Madam Vice-President, as a result of this exercise, Paraguay received 266 recommendations. Their analysis meant once again that our institutions had to undertake a significant amount of work. Each of the recommendations was distributed to the competent national institutions and examined individually, bearing in mind the content. the domestic legal framework, existing public policies, and the possibility of taking on board the commitment proposed. As a result of the process, Paraguay has accepted 238 recommendations, partially accepted three, and taken note of 25. Above all, these figures reflect my country's will continue to working on a broad human rights agenda. Amongst others, the recommendations encompass strengthening our institutions and Simorei+, reducing poverty, promoting social protection, access to justice, improving the prison system, combating human trafficking and child labor, freedom of expression, protecting journalists and human rights defenders, health, education, women's rights, the rights of children, adolescents, of indigenous peoples. of persons with disabilities, as well as protecting older persons and migrants. For my country, when we accept a recommendation, it means more than just agreeing with the proposal. It means that we take on board a commitment on which our institutions will have to work and then report back to you. And that is why we've worked to provide you with a thorough and transparent response. We decided to partially accept three of the recommendations because they contained various components which required differentiated responses. There were aspects which we could commit to and others which required a different position. There were 25 recommendations which we noted, and I'd like to explain why we took this decision. Taking note of a recommendation doesn't undermine a state's participation in the dialogue. It means that in the exact terms in which the recommendation of that state was formulated, Paraguay was not in a position to take on the commitment. And there are different reasons for this. For some of the recommendations, we found that they were incompatible with our constitution or our law in force. And others, there were concepts or categories which aren't mirrored in our domestic legal framework. And there are also recommendations which depicted our country in a different way to the way in which we see it, even though we maintain our commitment to continue to working in general on the problem which was highlighted. That's why our decision to accept or take note of a recommendation doesn't mean that this is our assessment of the state which made the recommendation. It's just a transparent way of showing that Paraguay, following the evaluation of the recommendation by our institutions, was in a position to accept it as a commitment or not. And we believe that being sincere also strengthens the UPR. A true dialogue among peers requires openness to listen to recommendations from others, but also the responsibility to clearly express which we are going to take on board and which we have a different position on. Paraguay has approached this process openly, respectfully and responsibly. Madam Vice-President, five years ago, we took a commitment before the Council to deploy efforts to translate recommendations into tangible action. Today we can look back on this period and we can see that many times Our work has led to significant change in our country, and we will continue to implement recommendations and tackle the challenges which have still not been resolved. We have a new series of recommendations before us today, and we will address them with the same spirit. I'd like to thank you for the time, attention, the contributions, all the states that took part in the review, and we're aware of the responsibility that we have with regard to your recommendations. And lastly, the true value of the UPI is not only measured by the number of recommendations accepted, but our ability to translate those commitments into stronger institutions, more effective public policies, better protection and enjoyment of human rights by all our citizens. It's in this belief that Paraguay once again reiterates its commitment to the UPR and the work which we must now carry out on the basis of the recommendations made by the Council. Thank you very much.
